title: Tuples, arrays, vectors, and maps with explicit contracts
summary: Choose a container by ownership, operations, ordering, and bounds; build a deterministic label report and explain scalar versus compound values.
objectives: Distinguish scalar values, tuples, arrays, vectors, slices, and UTF-8 text.
Use a borrowed slice when a function needs only sequence access.
Count bounded labels with HashMap and return owned deterministically ordered rows.
Separate input-size, distinct-key, text, and arithmetic limits.
body:
Purpose: choose a collection by the question it answers

The journal owns several tasks, and the log analyzer will count repeated categories. Before building those larger operations, learn the containers themselves. A fixed set of four measurements, an expandable sequence of tasks, and counts indexed by a label are different requirements. This lesson gives each a small explicit model, then connects ownership, lookup, ordering, and bounds to that choice. We will also fill in the scalar and compound vocabulary used throughout Rust documentation.

The runnable lab accepts at most 64 labels with at most eight distinct names. Names contain one through sixteen lowercase ASCII letters. It returns owned count rows in lexical order. Those limits are part of the contract, not assumptions hidden in a test fixture. The function builds a local result and publishes it only on success, so a rejected batch cannot expose a half-finished report.

Model: a scalar value or a compound value

A scalar represents one value: an integer, a floating-point number, a Boolean, or a char. You have used signed i64, unsigned u32, and bool. Signed integers permit negative values; unsigned ones do not. The number in an integer type is its bit width. usize is an unsigned, target-sized integer used for lengths and indexes. It is not a portable file-format field whose width you can assume. The earlier fractional converter introduces f64 and its approximation limits.

A Rust char, written with single quotes such as 'é', is one Unicode scalar value. A string, written with double quotes, contains UTF-8 encoded text. One scalar can occupy several UTF-8 bytes, and one user-perceived symbol can contain several scalars. Therefore “one char,” “one byte,” and “one visible symbol” are different claims. The example prints two UTF-8 bytes for 'é'. Our category grammar deliberately accepts ASCII letters, making its byte limit and accepted-character count coincide. The journal's broader UTF-8 title policy remains a separate contract.

A compound value groups other values. A tuple has a fixed number of positions, and its positions can have different types: (String, u32) pairs an owned label with its count. Access positions with .0 and .1, or destructure with let (label, count) = row;. A one-element tuple needs a comma, (value,); parentheses around value alone merely group an expression. The empty tuple () is the unit value encountered in function returns.

Arrays, vectors, and slices

An array has a fixed length and one element type. [i32; 4] means four signed 32-bit integers; [12, -8, 15, 9] constructs such an array. Length is part of its type, so an array of three values cannot replace an array of four in a parameter requiring exactly four. A vector, Vec<i32>, owns a growable sequence. vec![12, -8] creates one, and push appends. Its length is the number of initialized elements; its capacity concerns allocated room. They are related but not interchangeable.

A slice, &[i32], borrows a sequence without owning it or fixing its length in the function signature. Both an array and a vector can supply that view. Our sample_bounds needs to inspect values, not resize or retain their container, so it accepts a slice. This is a useful API habit: request the capability you need. Do not require &Vec<i32> when an array-backed caller can satisfy the same operation.

Indexing with values[index] requires a valid index and panics if it is out of bounds. A user-chosen index should normally go through get, returning Option. The lab's extrema function uses split_first to distinguish an empty slice before reading an element. It then compares each remaining value. This avoids inventing a “minimum” of zero, which would be wrong for an all-positive input, and avoids assuming there is always a first element.

Predict the observable result

Predict the extrema of [12, -8, 15, 9], the result for an empty slice, and the count rows for ["worker", "api", "api"]. Will changing the label input order change the count rows? Will eight distinct names followed by another occurrence of an existing name exceed the distinct-name limit? Write these answers before running. Separate a limit on input items from a limit on distinct keys.

mise exec -- cargo run -p core-rust-labs --example collections
mise exec -- cargo test -p core-rust-labs collections::

Run these reference commands from projects. The array and vector both produce Some((-8, 15)). The rows print api: 2 before worker: 1. An empty sample has no extrema and returns None. Repeating an existing key changes its count, not the number of distinct keys.

Read the complete checkpoint

HashMap associates a key with a value. Here a borrowed label is the key and a count is the value. Lookup asks “what count belongs to this label?” rather than “what sits at sequence position three?” The map's iteration order is not a stable presentation contract. We explicitly sort the final rows before returning them. That makes report order independent of the map's internal arrangement and of the input order for this counting task.

entry(label).or_insert(0) finds the existing count or inserts zero and returns access to that count. The dereference *count updates the number, not the local reference itself. The increment cannot overflow here: at most 64 input items can contribute. That local proof justifies ordinary addition. It would need revisiting if the API became an unbounded stream with a retained counter. A checked operation is necessary when the declared bounds do not establish the arithmetic range.

The map borrows labels only while the input remains available. Building the returned rows uses to_owned once per distinct label because callers should retain the report after the original strings disappear. This allocation serves a stated ownership requirement. The final comparison is a closure: |left, right| ... names two arguments to a small function supplied to sorting. It compares the first field of each tuple. We will study closure capture and iterator pipelines more deeply in the conversion lesson.

Guided construction with a reproducible source checkpoint

From the course root, make a complete standalone copy with the command below. The helper copies only this module and example, writes a standalone manifest with no dependencies, and refuses an existing destination. It does not copy build caches or silently replace earlier learner work. This gives you a known runnable checkpoint to compare against while you investigate.

python3 projects/reference/p18-core-labs/reconstruct.py collections --name collections-lab
cd learner-work/collections-lab
mise exec -- cargo run --example collections
mise exec -- cargo test

Now trace construction in three steps. First inspect sample_bounds and write the empty and single-element expectations before reading its loop. Second trace the count map after each of the three fixture labels; identify which insertion creates a new key. Third trace conversion to owned rows and sorting. In your copy, add one test where all values are positive and one where eight existing keys receive duplicates. Run those named tests, then the full package. Keep the first generated lockfile under version control.

Intentional mistake: use container order as business order

In a disposable learner edit, remove the explicit sorting step. This is deliberately outside the recommended contract. Your count totals may still be correct, and one run may even happen to print the expected order. Do not try to prove the problem by repeatedly running until luck produces a failure. The code now relies on an order the HashMap API does not promise. Review the documented iteration contract, restore sorting, and test equality after permuting input. A passing observation cannot strengthen an unspecified guarantee.

Playbook investigation: nine items exceed an eight-key limit

A report says nine labels were rejected even though “only eight are allowed.” That statement omits whether the limit concerns items or distinct names. Hypothesis A says the ninth item always fails. Hypothesis B says the ninth new key fails. Use eight different names plus a duplicate for one experiment, and the same prefix plus a new ninth name for another. The accepted duplicate disproves A. Preserve the input-item limit at 64 in both cases so it cannot explain the result.

Use the central playbook to record exact inputs, predicted result categories, and observed results. The repair may be a clearer error message or correcting a caller's expectation, rather than changing the bound. If a product now needs nine distinct categories, increasing the cap is a requirement change that needs memory and acceptance review. Your experiment distinguishes two policies for these inputs; it does not prove all possible text is valid.

Independent practice and separately revealed help

Add a query that returns the count for one requested label without changing the report. Specify whether an absent label returns zero or None, and whether an invalid query follows the same grammar as input labels. Then build a journal-status summary using a small vector of statuses and two counters. Explain why a two-variant enum may need no HashMap at all. Submit boundary cases, an ownership sketch, and one rejected alternative.

Hint 1: write the return contract first

Zero can be a useful display value, but None preserves the distinction between absent and explicitly stored zero. Choose one meaning before selecting a standard-library method.

Hint 2: separate observation from mutation

A query should not use an insertion path merely to obtain a default. For the fixed status enum, an exhaustive match can update the corresponding counter without allocating keys.

Reference approach after your attempt

A borrowed-map helper can use get and copy the small count, returning Option<u32>. For returned sorted rows, a simple bounded search is also appropriate; replacing the representation solely to optimize eight rows needs evidence. The two-status summary can use a pair of named counters and exhaustive matching. These are proposed extensions, not claims that the current reference already exposes those APIs.

Engineering decisions, evidence, and mastery

The slice parameter avoids unnecessary ownership requirements, local construction prevents partial-result publication, borrowed keys avoid repeated intermediate string allocation, and owned sorted output establishes lifetime and order guarantees. A BTreeMap is a reasonable alternative when ordered iteration is itself useful; it changes lookup and traversal costs. A small linear vector can also be appropriate at this bounded size. No timing comparison is asserted. The choice should follow required operations and measured scale, not a rule that hash maps are always faster.

Four focused tests cover slice sources, empty input, deterministic counts, independent resource limits, invalid text, and output ownership. Actual author checks are in the lab test log; independent review remains pending. To demonstrate mastery, choose a container for a changed requirement, explain the resulting ownership and ordering promises, and debug one failing boundary without reading the reference. A clean compile does not establish the business meaning of a count.

When you get stuck

Write the concrete element, key, and value types. Run only mise exec -- cargo test collections::tests::item_distinct_and_text_boundaries_are_independent in your learner package for a limit disagreement. Read the pinned HashMap entry and iteration documentation. Ask for review with the input list, distinct-key count, expected order, and one hypothesis your experiment disproved.

title: Validated conversions, standard traits, closures, and iterators
summary: Design a private validated type and preserve its meaning across From, TryFrom, parsing, formatting, and lazy batch processing.
objectives: Choose From or TryFrom according to conversion direction and possible failure.
Separate parsing grammar, domain validation, Display, and Debug.
Explain closure capture and Fn, FnMut, and FnOnce at the required API boundary.
Trace borrowed and owned iterator items and preserve errors through Result collection.
Explain module paths, visibility, executable documentation, and behavioral API compatibility.
Use TryInto through its TryFrom blanket implementation and make the destination type explicit.
body:
Purpose: conversion is a contract, not a convenient cast

Configuration values often arrive as strings or general integers, while the application needs a smaller valid domain. A percentage is a useful example: the storage type u8 accepts values through 255, but our whole-percentage contract permits only zero through one hundred. Merely changing an integer's type does not establish that rule. This lesson builds a validated percentage, gives standard traits distinct responsibilities, and then uses closures and iterators to process a batch without dropping errors.

This is a focused library checkpoint supporting the configuration project. It has no environment access, files, or networking. Input grammar is one through three ASCII decimal digits, with leading zeroes permitted. Fractions, signs, surrounding whitespace, and non-ASCII digits are rejected. The result is a whole percentage; the fractional length converter remains a separate domain with a different numeric model.

Plain model: lossless conversion, fallible conversion, and parsing

From<Source> for Destination describes an infallible conversion that fits the type's intended meaning. Our valid Percent always fits in a u16, so converting out is infallible. TryFrom returns a Result because converting a general u16 into a percentage can fail. These traits say more than the method name “convert”: callers can see whether failure must be handled. Implementing From also supplies the corresponding Into conversion through standard blanket implementations; normally implement the source-to-destination trait once.

FromStr handles parsing text. It separates accepted spelling from the numeric domain boundary. Display supplies the chosen user-facing spelling, and Debug supports developer inspection. Our error implements Display and std::error::Error so ordinary callers can preserve a structured error while choosing presentation. Those traits have different purposes; adding every standard trait automatically can accidentally promise behavior the type should not expose.

Percent(u8) is a newtype: a distinct type wrapping one value. Its field is private. External callers cannot construct Percent(255) directly, so the validation boundary is meaningful. It derives equality and ordering because ordinary numeric comparison matches the domain. It derives Copy and Clone because copying this tiny independent value has no ownership or resource-management consequence. A file handle or shared connection would require a different decision.

Predict before running

Predict the results of converting 100, 101, and 300 from u16. Then predict parsing "003", "+3", and "3.0". Which failures concern grammar, and which concern the valid percentage range? Finally predict whether displaying a value parsed from "003" preserves all three original characters. Write the contract before interpreting a surprising result.

mise exec -- cargo run -p core-rust-labs --example conversions
mise exec -- cargo test -p core-rust-labs conversions::

These reference commands run from projects. The example selects 25 and 100 percent, printing basis points [2500, 10000]. One basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point. The code multiplies a validated whole percentage by one hundred, so its maximum result is 10,000 and fits in u16. That bound justifies the arithmetic without adding a fallible operation that cannot fail under this type's invariant.

Read the complete conversion boundary

The TryFrom implementation checks the domain range before converting to the smaller storage type. Its remaining as u8 cast is justified by the immediately preceding proof: every admitted number is at most one hundred. A cast performed before that check could truncate a larger integer. The difference is the order of validation, not a blanket prohibition on the syntax as.

The parser first checks length and accepted digits. It then parses a u16, converts any syntax failure to the domain's syntax category, and calls the same validated constructor. It does not reproduce the range test in a second place. A future constructor can reuse TryFrom rather than creating another path into private storage. The Display implementation prints the numeric value, so "003" normalizes to "3". Value round-tripping holds; original-byte round-tripping is not promised.

In the example, let numeric: u16 = threshold.into(); gives type inference the destination. Without context, several conversions might be possible and the compiler can ask for an annotation. Such a diagnostic is not evidence that conversion failed at runtime. The program has not yet run. State the intended destination instead of adding arbitrary casts until compilation succeeds.

TryInto: the same checked conversion from the value side

The example writes let threshold: Percent = 25u16.try_into()?;. Read this as “try to convert this u16 into the destination type Percent.” The destination annotation matters because many types could accept an integer. Implementing TryFrom<u16> for Percent supplies the matching TryInto<Percent> through a standard-library blanket implementation: an implementation that applies to every type satisfying its stated trait bounds. We do not implement both sides separately. Percent::try_from(25u16) and 25u16.try_into() reach the same validation rule and return the same error for 101. Similarly, our From<Percent> for u16 supplies Into<u16>. Choose the spelling that makes the destination clearest in context. Neither spelling authorizes narrowing before checking, and the question-mark operator still propagates failure rather than inventing a replacement percentage.

Predict which annotation disappears if you write let threshold = Percent::try_from(25u16)?;, then make only that edit in your reconstructed example. The observed output and boundary tests should remain unchanged. This is a controlled comparison of two API spellings, not evidence that arbitrary numeric casts preserve the contract.

Closures: small functions that can capture context

A closure is a function-like value written with parameters between vertical bars: |value| expression. It can use values from its surrounding scope. The filter closure uses the threshold argument without receiving it as a second closure parameter; that is capture. Capture may borrow, mutably borrow, or own a value depending on use and explicit move. Adding move changes how captures enter the closure; it does not mean every captured value is deeply cloned.

The common callable traits describe how a closure can be invoked. FnOnce permits a call that consumes captured ownership; FnMut permits mutation of captured state between calls; Fn permits calling through shared access. A closure that only reads a copied threshold can satisfy the stronger reusable behavior. Choose bounds according to how the receiving function uses the callback. A one-time observation API should not demand an unnecessary reusable callback merely because a familiar example did so.

Iterators: a lazy sequence of operations

iter() visits borrowed elements. iter_mut() can visit mutable references when the container is mutably borrowed. into_iter() commonly consumes an owned container and yields owned elements. Always inspect the actual implementation and receiver type; an iterator is a protocol for obtaining items, not a promise that every method with a similar name moves the container. In this lab, keeping the caller's vector available is part of the contract, so we begin with borrowed iteration.

copied() changes references to our Copy percentages into independent small values. filter asks a predicate whether to retain an item; its predicate borrows the candidate, which explains the dereference in *value >= threshold. map transforms each retained value into basis points. These adapters are lazy: constructing the pipeline alone does not produce a new vector. collect() consumes it into the requested destination. Input order and duplicates survive unless an operation explicitly changes them.

The parser's destination is Result<Vec<Percent>, PercentError>. Collecting iterator items that are Results returns the first error instead of publishing a partial success. Compare this with a deliberately inappropriate filter_map(|text| text.parse().ok()): that would silently discard failed parses. A compact pipeline is only helpful when it preserves the required semantics. An ordinary loop returning early on error is equally valid and can be clearer when control flow grows.

Guided checkpoint: reconstruct, explain, modify

From the course root, create a complete standalone checkpoint. The helper refuses existing destinations and supplies the exact source and dependency-free manifest, so no hidden workspace inheritance is required.

python3 projects/reference/p18-core-labs/reconstruct.py conversions --name conversions-lab
cd learner-work/conversions-lab
mise exec -- cargo run --example conversions
mise exec -- cargo test

Trace the input ["25", "101", "bad"]. Mark the first successful constructor, the first error, and whether the final string is visited. Then temporarily express parse_percentages as an ordinary loop with ? and a local vector. Keep the same tests and error precedence. This is a guided equivalent implementation, not a claim that iterator syntax is inherently better. Explain the return type of every intermediate expression before choosing the version you find easier to review.

Intentional mistake: narrowing before validation

In your learner copy, intentionally narrow the input to u8 before comparing it with one hundred. Predict the result for the original u16 value 300. Integer narrowing retains only the representable low bits, producing 44 here, so the defective check admits an invalid original input. Run the constructor boundary test, observe the failing assertion, and restore validation before narrowing. Do not change the test to accept 44; the declared input was 300 percent.

Playbook investigation: the batch became shorter

A colleague changes Result collection to filter_map and reports that “the parser is more tolerant.” The observation is that three supplied strings produce two successful values without an error. Hypothesis A says iteration skipped a valid item. Hypothesis B says a parse failure was discarded. Compare an all-valid batch with a batch containing one invalid middle value, while keeping lengths equal. If only the invalid batch loses an item, the general iteration-skip explanation is disproved.

Use the playbook to record both returned values and error categories. Restore all-or-error behavior if that remains the requirement. If partial success is desired instead, return explicit per-item outcomes with positions; silently deleting an item changes correspondence to the caller's input. Your tests establish the chosen failure order for these cases. They do not establish that a future parallel implementation preserves that order automatically.

Independent practice with tiered hints

Add a validated RetryLimit newtype accepting integers from one through five. Support fallible construction from u16, lossless extraction to u16, and plain decimal display. Do not copy the percentage range accidentally. Then write a function selecting limits at or above a threshold, preserving order and duplicates. Include zero, one, five, six, and a narrowing-trap input such as 257. Explain why deriving Default might promise an invalid or arbitrary retry policy.

Hint 1: list construction routes

A private field is useful only if all public constructors enforce the same invariant. Write the accepted range beside every conversion direction.

Hint 2: make failure observable

The source integer can be invalid, so use TryFrom there. Every valid retry limit fits in u16, so From is appropriate in the other direction. Filter only validated values; do not filter away constructor errors.

Reference approach after your attempt

Validate (1..=5).contains(&value) before storing the value. Keep range rejection separate from text syntax if you also add parsing. A loop and a lazy adapter chain are both reasonable for selection if their output order and duplicates match the specification. This independent type is not included in the runnable Percent baseline.

Modules, public boundaries, and executable documentation

A Cargo package can contain a library crate and executable crates. A crate is a unit compiled by Rust; a module organizes names within that unit. In this lab, src/lib.rs declares pub mod conversions;, which loads the sibling src/conversions.rs module and exposes its name to users of the library. The example executable imports the public type through core_rust_labs::conversions::Percent. Cargo package names can contain hyphens; the Rust crate path uses underscores here. A module is not automatically another package or a network service.

The pub keyword makes an item visible through an accessible public path. Leaving a field private prevents outside callers from bypassing its constructor. pub(crate) can expose a helper across the current crate without promising it to downstream users. A use declaration brings a name into scope; it does not copy a module or install a dependency. Paths beginning crate:: start at the current crate root, while super:: refers to the parent module. The tests beside the implementation can reach details that external callers cannot, so they do not alone verify the public boundary.

Lines beginning /// document the following item. Rustdoc renders that documentation, and Cargo can compile its fenced Rust examples as documentation tests. Percent's example constructs a valid value and propagates its ordinary error with ?. The hidden final Result line gives the example an appropriate return type. Its separate compile_fail example tries to construct Percent(255) from outside the module; that is supposed to be rejected. Run mise exec -- cargo test --doc in the reconstructed package. A documented example that no longer compiles is a concrete interface defect, not a cosmetic documentation issue.

For a guided API change, add a named read-only getter to your learner type and add a documentation example calling it. Keep the private-field compile-fail test. Then review a proposal to change the accepted maximum from 100 to 80. It can preserve the Rust method signature while rejecting formerly valid callers, so signature compatibility alone does not establish behavioral compatibility. Conversely, adding a new public error variant can affect downstream exhaustive matches. State the old contract, affected clients, migration path, and tests before declaring an API change harmless. A private helper refactor that preserves the public contract has a narrower compatibility obligation.

Your independent review should distinguish four evidence sources: a module-local unit test can exercise internal cases; a separate executable or integration test uses exported paths; a documentation test checks the published example; and a compile-fail example checks a prohibited use. None establishes every future client behavior. For this small lab, the existing example executable and documentation examples exercise the public surface without adding an unnecessary separate framework.

Engineering decisions, evidence, and mastery

The chosen newtype makes a real range rule reusable; standard conversion and formatting traits let callers use familiar interfaces. Private storage and one fallible constructor prevent drift between entry points. The batch API preserves failure rather than hiding it behind a default. A simple validation function would be adequate for a one-off local calculation; a type earns its place when many functions should accept only validated values. Expanding to fractional percentages would require an explicit scale or numeric-model decision, not merely a formatting change.

Four unit tests cover constructor boundaries, normalization, first-error behavior, inclusive filtering, order, and duplicates. The actual lab checks are author evidence, not independent acceptance. For mastery, explain conversion direction, design a newtype for a different rule, translate a pipeline into a loop, and diagnose lost errors without copying the solution. Record both behavior and the reason that behavior is required.

When you get stuck

Write the iterator Item type after each adapter and the final collect type. Run mise exec -- cargo test conversions::tests::collection_reports_first_failure_instead_of_dropping_it. Read the pinned From, TryFrom, Iterator, and Result collection documentation. Bring a reviewer the original input, target type, failure policy, and smallest expression whose type or behavior surprised you.

Edition 2024: readable conditional bindings

Rust 1.88 stabilized let chains for edition 2024. A chain evaluates left to right and stops at the first failed match or false condition. Earlier bindings are available to later conditions and the successful branch. Use this when the conditions form one readable decision; use a match when the distinct failure cases need distinct handling.

From projects/, run mise exec -- cargo run -p core-rust-labs --example let_chains. Predict the outcome for missing, malformed, zero and positive input before running its assertions. This example intentionally collapses rejection causes into None; preserve Result in validation APIs when callers need those causes. Nested if-let remains valid Rust.

title: Cell and RefCell: shared ownership with checked access
summary: Give two synchronous callbacks one bounded audit buffer, then investigate dynamic borrow conflicts, snapshots, and guard cleanup.
objectives: Separate Rc shared ownership from Cell and RefCell mutation mechanisms.
Return ordinary errors for reachable dynamic borrow conflicts.
Trace RefCell guard lifetime through nested callbacks and unwinding.
Justify interior mutability against exclusive ownership and a new cross-thread requirement.
Distinguish strong and weak ownership, handle failed upgrades, and identify reference-count cycles in a proposed callback graph.
body:
Purpose: share one small state without hiding the ownership cost

Suppose two synchronous callbacks need to retain handles to the same local audit buffer. They record short messages and can temporarily disable recording. A single exclusive owner passing &mut Vec would be the simplest design if the callbacks did not need independently retained handles. Here that lifetime requirement is explicit, so the lab uses reference-counted ownership and controlled interior mutability. This is a single-threaded example; concurrency remains a separate design problem.

The buffer stores at most four messages, each one through 64 UTF-8 bytes with no control characters. Every call validates its message, even when recording is disabled. A valid disabled call returns Ok(false); an accepted record returns Ok(true). Invalid input, a full buffer, and a conflicting runtime borrow are distinct errors. These rules keep the example small while making the hard questions observable.

Plain model: ownership and permission to mutate are different

Rc supplies shared ownership within one thread. Cloning its handle adds another owner of the same allocation; it does not clone the inner vector of messages. The inner allocation remains alive while any strong owner remains. Shared ownership alone does not permit arbitrary mutation through a shared reference. That distinction matters: an ownership wrapper answers “who keeps this alive?” while a mutation mechanism answers “when may the contents change?”

Cell<bool> stores the enabled flag. Reading with get copies a small Boolean out; setting replaces that value. The API does not lend an ordinary reference to the inner Boolean that could be invalidated by a later replacement. This fits a small Copy value. RefCell<Vec<String>> instead provides checked temporary access to a larger non-Copy value. It tracks shared and exclusive borrows at runtime while preserving the essential rule that mutable access cannot coexist with another active access to the same contents.

This is called interior mutability: an API can mutate controlled contents through &self. It is not a compiler escape hatch. Safe standard-library APIs enforce the relevant rules, and the compiler still constrains how returned guards and references are used. RefCell does not become a thread-safe lock, and wrapping it in an atomic reference counter would not automatically fix that limitation. The lesson's compile-fail doctest makes the single-threaded boundary explicit.

Prediction: a callback tries to write while reading

The first callback records “first callback”; the second records “second callback.” An observer then reads both messages while trying to record a third through another handle. Predict whether the third record succeeds, blocks, panics, or returns an error. Finally disable recording and submit a valid message. Does disabled recording mean an invalid message is now accepted? Write the expected result category and resulting message list for each step.

mise exec -- cargo run -p core-rust-labs --example interior
mise exec -- cargo test -p core-rust-labs interior::
mise exec -- cargo test -p core-rust-labs --doc

Run from projects. The observer sees two messages. The reentrant write returns Err(Borrowed). The later valid disabled call returns false, and the snapshot still has the original two messages. There is no thread waiting for another thread here. The conflict is caused by an observer's still-live shared borrow during a nested call.

Read the complete safe implementation

SharedAudit exposes methods while its Inner fields remain private. Default constructs a fresh enabled buffer. Deriving Clone for the outer handle clones the Rc, deliberately sharing the same Inner. The name “shared” therefore describes an actual observable relationship, verified by a test that disables recording through one handle and records through another. Dropping one handle does not invalidate the other owner.

record validates text before any buffer mutation. It then reads the Cell flag. If disabled, it returns without requesting a mutable vector borrow. Otherwise try_borrow_mut obtains a guard or reports a conflict. Mapping that conflict into AuditError::Borrowed makes it part of the method's normal Result contract. Only after checking capacity does the function allocate its owned message and push it. A rejected operation leaves the existing message list intact.

The local messages guard dereferences to the vector for its operations. Its Drop releases the runtime borrow when the scope ends, including an ordinary early return. This connects directly to the RAII lesson: a guard's lifetime is the permission interval. Keeping the guard alive longer than necessary can prevent useful work even though every operation remains memory-safe. Do not infer the interval only from where the programmer last thinks about the variable; inspect its actual scope and uses.

Observation, snapshots, and callback contracts

with_messages accepts impl FnOnce(&[String]) -> R. The caller supplies one computation over a borrowed view, and the method returns that computation's result. FnOnce is sufficient because the callback is invoked once. The shared borrow guard stays alive while it runs. Calling record inside that callback therefore cannot obtain the exclusive borrow, and our fallible API reports the conflict. The observer should be short and synchronous; this is not an async synchronization primitive.

snapshot uses the same observation boundary to clone the bounded messages into an owned vector. A snapshot costs allocations, but the caller can then process it after the shared borrow ends. That is a reasonable alternative when downstream work may call back into the logger. Avoid declaring either approach universally superior. Borrowed observation avoids the copy but constrains reentrancy; owned observation buys independent lifetime with an explicit bounded cost.

A callback panic is not one of record's ordinary error outcomes. The dedicated test deliberately panics inside observation, catches that unwind in the test harness, and then records successfully. This checks guard cleanup during unwinding. It does not promise rollback of every effect a callback performed before panicking, and a build configured to abort on panic would not continue. Production logic should not use caught panic as its routine borrowing-control protocol.

Weak observers and ownership cycles

Sometimes a callback registration should find a buffer only while another part of the program owns it. Retaining a strong SharedAudit would extend the buffer lifetime. WeakAudit instead holds Weak<Inner>: a non-owning link created with Rc::downgrade. Its upgrade method returns Option<SharedAudit>. Some gives the caller a new strong owner; None means all strong owners have already gone away. The weak allocation bookkeeping can remain until weak handles disappear, but the messages themselves are dropped when the final strong owner disappears. A weak handle is therefore not a borrowed reference that you can dereference indefinitely.

Predict the final line of the example before running it. Both callback handles are explicitly dropped, so the observer prints false. In the lifetime test, dropping the first owner still permits an upgrade because the second owner exists. The temporary upgraded handle is dropped at the end of its assertion statement. Only then do we drop the second owner and require None. If you save that upgraded handle in a local variable, you have introduced another strong owner; an unexpected successful later upgrade would be explained by that ownership fact. Record a diagram of live handles before concluding that Weak leaked the buffer.

A reference-count cycle arises when object A strongly owns B and B strongly owns A. Removing outside handles leaves each count nonzero; reference counting alone cannot infer that the cycle is unreachable. Our buffer contains strings, not stored callbacks or parent links, so this implementation has no such cycle. If a future observer registry stores callbacks that capture the buffer strongly, that new graph requires review. Prefer a clear owner and a weak back-reference when the observer must not extend the owner lifetime; require the callback to handle a failed upgrade. Weak is not a universal repair: an edge that represents real required ownership must remain strong. Draw the graph and state who is responsible for keeping each object alive.

Intentional mistake: replacing an ordinary error with a panic

In a disposable learner edit, replace try_borrow_mut and its error mapping with borrow_mut. Predict the reentrant-write test. The infallible-looking API panics on the conflicting borrow, so a caller expecting Err(Borrowed) no longer receives the promised outcome. Run that one test and restore the original fallible call. The lesson is not that borrow_mut is always forbidden; it is inappropriate where a reachable caller behavior is documented as an ordinary error.

A different deliberate mistake is holding a mutable guard and then invoking arbitrary user callbacks before releasing it. That enlarges the reentrancy surface and makes the permission interval harder to reason about. Our record method calls no user callback while mutably borrowed. Review this structural choice before proposing broad panic handling or a larger wrapper hierarchy.

Playbook investigation: “two owners copied my messages”

You see identical messages through two handles and suspect that Clone copied the vector. Competing hypotheses are independent copied storage and shared storage behind two ownership handles. Disable recording through the first handle, attempt a valid record through the second, then re-enable through the second. If the setting affects both handles and a later record is visible from both, the independent-copy explanation is disproved. A test that only compares their initial contents could not distinguish those designs.

Next investigate a Borrowed error. A plausible but incorrect diagnosis is that another operating-system thread still holds a lock. Reproduce it with one thread and a nested observation callback. The same error without spawning any thread disproves that diagnosis. The fix can shorten the observation scope or use a bounded snapshot before reentrant work. Independent practice and tiered hints

Add a fallible drain operation that transfers all retained messages to an owned vector and leaves the live buffer empty. Decide whether draining while disabled is allowed; the flag currently controls recording, not observation. Require Borrowed when a shared observer is active, and require the old messages to remain intact after that rejection. Test an empty buffer, a full buffer, a blocked drain, a successful drain, and recording again afterward. This is an extension beyond the supplied baseline.

Hint 1: identify the permission needed

Moving messages out changes the vector, so a shared borrow is insufficient. Obtain a fallible mutable guard before changing the state. Disabled recording need not prevent an explicitly separate maintenance operation.

Hint 2: preserve ownership without cloning

Once exclusive access exists, consider std::mem::take on the vector. It replaces the stored vector with its default empty value and returns the previously owned one. No message-by-message clone is required.

Reference approach after your attempt

The operation can map try_borrow_mut failure to Borrowed, take the vector, and return it. Document the enabled-flag policy before testing. A rejected borrow does not execute the take, so the original buffer survives. Returning an owned vector also prevents callers from retaining a reference into a buffer that will later be reused. This direction still requires your own implementation and tests.

Engineering decisions, evidence, and mastery

One small Cell fits an independent Copy flag; one RefCell protects the vector; Rc satisfies the two-callback lifetime requirement; private fields keep validation and bounds centralized. Plain exclusive ownership is the preferable alternative when independently retained handles are unnecessary. A cross-thread requirement would call for a new ownership and synchronization design, with Send/Sync, contention, cancellation, and shutdown review. Merely exchanging wrapper names is not an architecture.

Four native tests exercise shared identity, bounds and rejection preservation, reentrancy, and guard cleanup on unwind. A compile-fail doctest rejects transferring this Rc-backed handle into a spawned thread. See the actual test evidence. Tests cover chosen traces; they do not prove every callback is well-behaved. Author verification and independent review are separate, and no browser behavior is claimed.

For mastery, explain which wrapper supplies ownership, which supplies access checking, and why a dynamic borrow conflict can happen in one thread. Implement drain under your stated flag policy, demonstrate rejected-state preservation, and compare an observation callback with an owned snapshot.
